questions.question: Can you modify a map's values while ranging over it?
questions.title: Can You Modify A Map's Values While
questions.direct_answer: Yes — updating existing keys during range is allowed. Adding new keys during iteration is unspecified; deleting is safe.

sections.title: Quick Revision

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    MK[make map K V] --> W{write to nil map?}
    W -->|yes| PANIC[panic: assignment to entry in nil map]
    W -->|no| OK[keys hash into buckets]
    LIT[map literal] --> READY[write-ready from birth]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The rules differ because the operations differ. Updating m[k] inside range m doesn't restructure anything — the key exists, the value slot exists, the write is just a store. The iterator is walking buckets, and stores to existing entries don't move them.

Deletion during iteration is tolerated with a relaxed contract: entries deleted ahead of the iterator's position may or may not be visited — the spec says unspecified, meaning 'the runtime may differ, don't depend on it.' What's guaranteed: no crash, no corruption, and entries that exist and aren't deleted will all be seen. The cleanup loop pattern (range + delete expired) is standard idiom precisely because those guarantees are enough.

Insertion is where the runtime refuses to promise anything at all: a new key may land in a bucket the iterator already passed (never visited) or hasn't reached (may be visited) — and with growth, the iterator might follow a growing structure indefinitely. An infinite loop is constructible, and the code that has one looks innocent:

```go
for k := range m {
    m[k+"-new"] = process(m[k])   // adds keys forever in the worst shapes
}
```
The fix pattern: collect the additions, apply them after the loop — two passes, deterministic, and the intent is visible in the shape.

questions.question: Does range copy the slice?
questions.title: Does Range Copy The Slice
questions.direct_answer: range evaluates the slice expression once — copying the header. Length is fixed at loop start: appends inside the loop are invisible to it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Range Over Slice Map.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: range evaluates the slice expression once — copying the header.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The range expression is evaluated exactly once, at loop start. For a slice, that means the header — pointer, length, capacity — is copied once into the loop's internal state. The elements are not copied; the loop reads through the pointer.

The observable consequence: the loop's length is frozen at entry. Appends inside the body grow a different (new) backing array — the loop keeps walking the original header's extent:

```go
s := []int{1, 2, 3}
for i, v := range s {
    s = append(s, v*10)      // grows s — the loop doesn't see it
    fmt.Println(i, v)
}
fmt.Println(len(s))  // 6 — the appends DID land, after the loop's snapshot
```

Three iterations, not six — the loop captured len 3 at start. This is why range-over-slice can't infinite-loop on self-append the way some for-loops in other languages can.

The same once-only rule explains the nested pattern: ranging s and ranging s[i] inside — each inner range snapshots its own expression, and neither is affected by outer-body changes to s's length. It's consistent: one evaluation, one snapshot, every range.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SRC[s: 1 2 3] --> CPY[copy or append-nil idiom]
    CPY --> DST[u: 1 2 3 — NEW storage]
    M[u 0 = 50] --> DST
    SRC2[s still 1 2 3] -.independent.-> SRC
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The once-only evaluation is the language rule that makes loop semantics stable: 'The range expression x is evaluated once before beginning the loop.' For a slice, that evaluation yields the header (pointer, len, cap) — and the loop's internal snapshot is that header.

The append-invisibility follows mechanically: appends that fit in capacity write into the SAME backing array — the loop, walking its snapshot pointer, DOES see those in-place writes to elements it hasn't reached. But appends that grow the slice allocate a new array — the loop's snapshot still points at the old one — and those elements are invisible.

So the precise statement is subtler than 'appends are invisible': in-capacity appends to not-yet-visited indices ARE seen (shared storage); growth appends are not (forked storage). Both facts fall out of the header snapshot:

```go
s := make([]int, 3, 10)
for i, v := range s {
    s = append(s, 99)      // in-capacity: writes backing[3..]
    _ = v
    fmt.Println(i)          // 0 1 2 — the snapshot's len, never more
}
```
The loop length froze at 3; the shared-array writes happened where the loop never looks. Range can't loop forever on self-append — the frozen len is the safety.

questions.question: What is the classic range gotcha with loop variables (pre Go 1.22)?
questions.title: Classic Range Gotcha With Loop Variables (pre
questions.direct_answer: Before 1.22, the loop variable was ONE reused variable — closures and goroutines capturing it saw the last value. 1.22 gives each iteration a fresh variable.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why did the old semantics exist at all? Performance — one variable, one address, reused: the loop didn't allocate per iteration. The cost was that the single-address decision leaked into closures, and closures capture by reference in Go. The two features composed into the most common Go bug of the 2010s.

The 1.22 fix is a rare breaking-ish change the Go team could make because the old behavior was almost never intended — the proposals (years of them) documented that the capture bug dominated every legitimate use of the shared variable. The compatibility promise bent to reality: code relying on the old behavior was almost certainly broken code.

For interviews and code review today: mention the version. 'Each iteration gets a fresh variable since 1.22' is the current truth; 'capture the loop variable in a goroutine and you'll see the last value' is the historical truth that explains why old code is full of pass-through parameters and why linters still flag the pattern. Both halves are knowledge; the version boundary is where they meet.
